targets.title: Polynomial Codes Over Certain Finite Fields
targets.venue: Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
targets.why_needed: Origin of Reed-Solomon codes, the maximum-distance-separable construction every later erasure-coded storage system (Storj, Sia, Xorbas, Azure LRC, Clay codes) uses or benchmarks against for the storage-overhead-versus-fault-tolerance tradeoff at overhead n/k.

targets.title: A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function
targets.why_needed: Origin of the hash tree construction underlying every content-addressed, Merkle-linked data structure (IPFS's IPLD, Git, Filecoin's sector proofs) that lets a verifier check one leaf against a small path of hashes rather than downloading the whole structure.

targets.title: LT Codes
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
targets.why_needed: First practical rateless fountain code: a sender produces an unbounded stream of coded symbols from k source symbols and any (1+epsilon)k of them suffice to decode, with no fixed rate n/k to pre-select. Foundational for Raptor and RaptorQ, and the alternative to fixed-rate Reed-Solomon for object delivery over an unreliable channel of unknown loss rate.

targets.title: Raptor Codes
targets.why_needed: Concatenates an outer fixed-rate code with an inner LT code to make decoding cost linear in k and overhead approach zero as k grows, fixing LT codes' non-linear decode cost. The basis of RaptorQ (RFC 6330) and of every fountain-code argument for encoding storage objects once and letting any sufficient subset of coded pieces reconstruct them, independent of which pieces are held by which peers.

targets.title: RaptorQ Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery
targets.authors: Michael Luby, Amin Shokrollahi, Mark Watson, Thomas Stockhammer, Lorenz Minder
targets.why_needed: The deployed rateless-code standard: states decoding failure probability at exactly k received symbols (roughly 1%) and at k+1 or k+2 (roughly 0.01% and near-zero), and the block and sub-symbol size parameters used in production object-delivery systems. Sets the concrete failure-probability-versus-overhead curve a fountain-coded storage design should be checked against, rather than an assumed one.

targets.title: Network Coding for Distributed Storage Systems
targets.authors: Alexandros G. Dimakis, P. Brighten Godfrey, Yunnan Wu, Martin J. Wainwright, Kannan Ramchandran
targets.why_needed: Origin of regenerating codes: derives the storage-versus-repair-bandwidth tradeoff curve for reconstructing one lost coded piece from d helper nodes, and states the two extreme points on that curve — Minimum-Storage Regenerating (MSR, storage overhead equal to plain erasure coding, higher repair bandwidth) and Minimum-Bandwidth Regenerating (MBR, higher storage overhead, lowest possible repair bandwidth). This is the tradeoff curve every later construction (product-matrix, Clay, LRC, convertible) is checked against.

targets.title: Optimal Exact-Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage at the MSR and MBR Points via a Product-Matrix Construction
targets.authors: K. V. Rashmi, Nihar B. Shah, P. Vijay Kumar
targets.why_needed: First explicit code construction that hits both MSR and MBR points with exact repair (the repaired piece is bit-for-bit identical to the lost one, not merely functionally equivalent), for all storage-overhead parameters, at the cost of a minimum-helper-count requirement d >= 2k-1 for MSR. States that requirement explicitly, which is the exact number a liveness objection to regenerating codes (any k of n survive storage, but a repair needs d of n-1 remaining pieces simultaneously reachable) must be checked against.

targets.title: Locally Repairable Codes
targets.authors: Dimitris S. Papailiopoulos, Alexandros G. Dimakis
targets.why_needed: Defines locality r: the number of other coded pieces that must be read to reconstruct one lost piece, distinct from the regenerating-code d (number of helper nodes contacted). Proves a Singleton-type bound coupling locality, minimum distance, and storage overhead, and shows locality can be small (independent of n) at a fixed storage-overhead cost. This is what a repair-liveness objection to regenerating codes (needing d of n-1 pieces live) can be traded against: lower r means fewer pieces to contact per repair, at a different overhead price than MSR/MBR.

targets.title: Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage
targets.authors: Cheng Huang, Huseyin Simitci, Yikang Xu, Aaron Ogus, Brad Calder, Parikshit Gopalan, Jin Li, Sergey Yekhanin
targets.why_needed: Deployed measurement of a locally repairable code (Azure's LRC) running in production storage, reporting reconstruction I/O and repair bandwidth reduction relative to Reed-Solomon at a stated storage-overhead cost. The reference point for what locality gains look like outside a simulation, cited by nearly every later locally-repairable-code paper as its deployed baseline.

targets.title: XORing Elephants: Novel Erasure Codes for Big Data
targets.authors: Maheswaran Sathiamoorthy, Megasthenis Asteris, Dimitris S. Papailiopoulos, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Ramkumar Vadali, Scott Chen, Dhruba Borthakur
targets.why_needed: Deployed measurement of the Xorbas locally repairable code running on a Facebook production Hadoop cluster, reporting disk I/O and repair network traffic reduction against plain Reed-Solomon at a stated cluster scale. A second deployed data point (alongside Azure LRC) for what a locality-versus-overhead choice returns on a real repair workload, from a different operator and workload than Azure's.

targets.title: Clay Codes: Moulding MDS Codes to Yield an MSR Code
targets.authors: Myna Vajha, Vinayak Ramkumar, Bhagyashree Puranik, Ganesh R. Kini, Elita A. Lobo, Birenjith Sasidharan, P. Vijay Kumar, Alexander Barg, Min Ye, Srinivasan Narayanamurthy, Syed Hussain, Siddhartha Nandi
targets.venue: USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies (FAST)
targets.why_needed: Construction that produces a minimum-storage-regenerating code from any Maximum-Distance-Separable code by pairwise-coupling scalar values ("coupled-layer" transform), reported deployed in Ceph, with measured repair-bandwidth reduction against Reed-Solomon at production scale. Directly competes with the product-matrix construction (RASHMI-TIT-11) on the same MSR point and is the deployed alternative construction whose reported numbers the product-matrix numbers must be checked against.

targets.title: Convertible Codes: Enabling Efficient Conversion of Coded Data in Distributed Storage
targets.why_needed: Defines code conversion: changing an already-stored object's erasure-code parameters (for example raising or lowering storage overhead as durability requirements change) without a full re-encode from the original data. States the bandwidth cost of conversion as a function of the before and after parameters, which bears directly on repair economics because a repair after partial data loss is a special case of conversion (converting from a degraded to a full parameter set).

targets.title: Locally Repairable Convertible Codes: Erasure Codes for Efficient Repair and Conversion
targets.venue: IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT)
targets.why_needed: Combines locally repairable codes and convertible codes into one construction, so repairing a lost piece and later converting the object's storage-overhead parameters both cost less than treating them as separate operations under the prior separate constructions. A 2023 result directly answering the brief's search for work lowering the resource cost of repair since the 2010-2018 regenerating/locally-repairable code line.

targets.title: Locally Repairable Convertible Codes With Optimal Access Costs
targets.why_needed: An independently authored 2024 construction in the same locally-repairable-convertible-code space as MATURANA-ISIT-23, optimizing the count of pieces accessed during conversion rather than bandwidth. A second, independent construction whose optimality claims and access-cost numbers the Maturana-Rashmi line must be checked against.

targets.title: Tight Lower Bounds and Optimal Constructions of Locally Repairable Convertible Codes in the Split Regime
targets.why_needed: June 2026 result proving a lower bound on conversion bandwidth in the split regime (one stored object's parameters split into several with different parameters) and a construction meeting it, closing a gap left open by the 2023-2025 locally-repairable-convertible-code papers. Confirms the sub-field was still moving in the two months before this pass, so any bandwidth-optimality claim taken from an earlier LRCC paper needs checking against this bound.

targets.title: Generalized Regenerating Codes and Node Repair on Graphs
targets.why_needed: Extends regenerating codes from the standard model (any d of the remaining n-1 nodes can serve as helpers, all links equal) to an arbitrary graph in which only specified nodes can communicate and links carry nonuniform capacities. Directly relevant to the repair-liveness objection to regenerating codes: it replaces the requirement 'd specific live holders reachable' with a requirement stated over whichever holders the network graph actually connects, which is a materially different and possibly weaker liveness condition depending on the graph's structure.

targets.title: Erasure Coding Vs. Replication: A Quantitative Comparison
targets.why_needed: First quantitative comparison of whole-copy replication against erasure coding for a peer-to-peer storage system at matched durability, reporting the storage-overhead and repair-bandwidth cost of each at stated node-availability levels. One of two independent papers (with RODRIGUES-IPTPS-05) making this comparison; the brief requires holding both since competing papers frequently disagree on the numbers.

targets.title: High Availability in DHTs: Erasure Coding vs. Replication
targets.why_needed: A second, independent replication-versus-erasure-coding comparison, run three years after WEATHERSPOON-IPTPS-02 with a distributed-hash-table-specific availability model, reporting the repair-bandwidth crossover point at which erasure coding stops being cheaper than replication as node availability drops. Holds the comparison numbers from a different research group under a different availability model, which the brief requires be checked against the first paper's numbers rather than assumed to agree.

targets.title: High Availability, Scalable Storage, Dynamic Peer Networks: Pick Two
targets.venue: Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS)
targets.why_needed: Derives a lower bound on the per-node bandwidth a peer-to-peer storage system needs for repair, as a function of measured node session length (churn rate), stored data volume per node, and target durability, and shows the bound is violated by then-typical residential upload bandwidth at then-measured churn rates. The formula is the one a repair-economics claim for any erasure-coded storage design must be run through with the design's own n, k, and measured churn rate as inputs, rather than asserted qualitatively.

targets.title: Efficient Replica Maintenance for Distributed Storage Systems
targets.authors: Byung-Gon Chun, Frank Dabek, Andreas Haeberlen, Emil Sit, Hakim Weatherspoon, M. Frans Kaashoek, John Kubiatowicz, Robert Morris
targets.venue: USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI)
targets.why_needed: The Carbonite system: measures repair bandwidth on a live PlanetLab deployment under real node churn traces and shows that repairing every transient failure (as a naive scheme does) drives repair bandwidth far above the durability-necessary minimum; introduces a repair policy that defers repair for short-lived departures and reports the resulting bandwidth reduction against the naive policy on the same trace. Directly supplies the measured-churn repair-traffic figures the brief's repair-economics question requires.

targets.title: Total Recall: System Support for Automated Availability Management
targets.authors: Ranjita Bhagwan, Kiran Tati, Yuchung Cheng, Stefan Savage, Geoffrey M. Voelker
targets.venue: USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI)
targets.why_needed: System that continuously measures each node's observed availability and adjusts per-object redundancy (replication or erasure-coding rate) to a target durability, reporting the resulting repair-bandwidth cost against a fixed-redundancy baseline under a real availability trace. The paper CHUN-NSDI-06 explicitly responds to and improves on, so holding both supplies the before-and-after repair-bandwidth numbers for the same design question.

targets.title: Understanding Availability
targets.authors: Ranjita Bhagwan, Stefan Savage, Geoffrey M. Voelker
targets.why_needed: Measures host availability (fraction of time online) across a large deployed peer-to-peer system (Overnet) and reports the distribution's shape and its implication for how availability should be modeled in a repair-economics calculation, as opposed to assuming a single mean availability figure. The churn-rate input BLAKE-HOTOS-03's bandwidth bound and CHUN-NSDI-06's repair-policy design both need, from a system independent of either.

targets.title: The Computational and Storage Potential of Volunteer Computing
targets.venue: IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Cluster Computing and the Grid (CCGrid)
targets.why_needed: Measures disk space, availability, and churn across more than 330,000 hosts in a deployed volunteer-computing project (BOINC), reporting the aggregate storage capacity those hosts could supply and the fraction actually reachable at any moment. The direct measurement the brief's 'what does volunteer storage actually supply' question calls for, from hosts running unmodified consumer software rather than a research testbed.

targets.title: PORs: Proofs of Retrievability for Large Files
targets.authors: Ari Juels, Burton S. Kaliski Jr.
targets.venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: Defines proof of retrievability: a storage provider proves, via a compact challenge-response exchange, that it still holds a specific file in full, without transmitting the file. Introduces the use of embedded random-check blocks (sentinels) mixed into an erasure-coded encoding of the file so an incorrect response to a spot check statistically implies data has been altered or lost. States the security bound as a function of the fraction of the file corrupted and the number of sentinels checked.

targets.title: Compact Proofs of Retrievability
targets.why_needed: Improves on JUELS-CCS-07 with a homomorphic authenticator construction that lets a verifier combine many blocks' authenticators into one short response, stated to shrink communication per challenge from linear to constant in the number of blocks checked, and gives the first proof-of-retrievability scheme with a formal security proof. The construction whose asymptotic communication-cost claim a repair-and-audit design should be checked against rather than the earlier sentinel scheme.

targets.title: Provable Data Possession at Untrusted Stores
targets.authors: Giuseppe Ateniese, Randal C. Burns, Reza Curtmola, Joseph Herring, Lea Kissner, Zachary N. J. Peterson, Dawn Song
targets.venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: Introduces provable data possession, a different guarantee than proof of retrievability: the provider proves possession of most of the file via homomorphic tags checked over a random block sample, without the file being reconstructible from the proof exchange, and without necessarily proving the client could reconstruct the whole file if some blocks were in fact lost. The paper whose weaker-guarantee-but-lower-cost tradeoff a proof-of-retrievability design should be checked against by name, since the two guarantees are frequently conflated.

targets.title: Proofs of Space
targets.authors: Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust, Vladimir Kolmogorov, Krzysztof Pietrzak
targets.why_needed: Defines proof of space: a prover commits disk space by computing a hard-to-invert function of that size once, then answers later challenges cheaply, proving continued possession of the space without repeating the expensive computation. The primitive underlying proof-of-spacetime schemes (used by Filecoin and Chia) for proving storage over an interval of time without a per-challenge full rescan of the stored data.

targets.title: Tight Proofs of Space and Replication
targets.why_needed: Formal treatment of proof of replication: a provider proves it stores n independent physical replicas of the same data (not one copy referenced n times) by proving each replica took at least a stated sequential computation time to produce from the data, with a formally proved lower bound on the adversary's cheating probability as a function of replica count and per-replica encoding depth. The academic construction underlying Filecoin's deployed Proof-of-Replication, stated with a security proof the whitepaper (BENET-FILECOIN-17) does not itself provide.

targets.title: IPFS - Content Addressed, Versioned, P2P File System
targets.why_needed: Origin description of the content-addressing mechanism underlying the InterPlanetary File System: every object is named by the cryptographic hash of its bytes, linked into a Merkle directed acyclic graph so that any subtree can be verified without re-hashing the whole graph, retrieved from any peer holding it via a distributed hash table keyed by that same hash. States the mechanism a person can implement; measured deployment behavior is in TRAUTWEIN-SIGCOMM-22.

targets.title: Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web
targets.authors: Dennis Trautwein, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro, Will Scott, Moritz Schubotz, Bela Gipp, Yiannis Psaras
targets.why_needed: Deployed measurement of the live IPFS network's content-lookup and retrieval performance and content-popularity distribution, run against the network's actual population rather than a simulation, and identifies which components of the design (Bitswap block exchange, the Kademlia distributed hash table) dominate observed latency. The measurement study a content-addressing design's latency claims must be checked against.

targets.title: Tahoe: The Least-Authority Filesystem
targets.venue: ACM Workshop on Storage Security and Survivability (StorageSS)
targets.why_needed: Deployed system combining erasure coding for durability with per-file capability-based encryption keys derived from the file's own content hash, so that possessing a read capability to a file is both the decryption key and the means of locating it, with no separate access-control server. States the specific erasure-code parameters used in production (3-of-10 default) and the storage-overhead-versus-durability tradeoff that setting implies.

targets.title: SoK: Decentralized Storage Network
targets.authors: Chuanlei Li, Minghui Xu, Jiahao Zhang, Hechuan Guo, Xiuzhen Cheng
targets.why_needed: 2024 systematization of knowledge across deployed decentralized storage networks (the brief's explicit ask for a post-2023 SoK in this area), classifying their storage-verification mechanisms (proof of replication, proof of spacetime, proof of storage), redundancy schemes, and incentive designs on a common set of axes. Use to check that no major deployed system or mechanism family is missing from this target list before closing out domain C.

targets.title: Filecoin: A Decentralized Storage Network
targets.why_needed: Describes the deployed pairing of Proof-of-Replication (a storage provider proves n independent physical copies of client data) and Proof-of-Spacetime (the provider repeats a cheap proof at intervals, so a provider that deletes the data fails the next one) as the verification layer behind a market matching clients wanting durability against providers offering disk space, with the specific sealing and window-post proof intervals used in production. The deployed system FISCH-EUROCRYPT-19 supplies the formal security treatment for.

targets.title: Sia: Simple Decentralized Storage
targets.why_needed: Describes a storage-contract design in which a client and a storage host jointly sign a smart-contract-style agreement specifying data, price, and a schedule of storage proofs, settled without a third-party escrow. A different incentive-and-verification structure than Filecoin's for the same underlying proof-of-storage problem, needed to compare the two mechanisms' cost and trust assumptions rather than treat Filecoin's design as the only deployed answer.

targets.title: Storj: A Decentralized Cloud Storage Network Framework
targets.authors: Shawn Wilkinson and Storj Labs, Inc.
targets.why_needed: Describes a design that erasure-codes each file, distributes pieces to independent storage nodes under per-piece audit contracts, and states a target storage-overhead ratio for the deployed network. A third deployed erasure-coded storage design (alongside Filecoin's replication-based and Sia's contract-based approaches) whose stated overhead figure needs checking against what the network's own repair mechanism requires to sustain it, per the brief's ban on taking a single deployed system's parameter as the only possible value.

targets.title: Arweave: A Protocol for Economically Sustainable Information Permanence
targets.authors: Sam Williams, Viktor Diordiiev, Lev Berman, Ivan Uemlianin
targets.why_needed: Describes a design that pays once for storage intended to persist indefinitely, using a proof-of-access consensus rule that requires each block producer to present a copy of a randomly selected past block before it can produce a new one, which is stated to reward replication of rarely accessed old data rather than only frequently requested recent data. A durability model structurally different from Filecoin's, Sia's, and Storj's per-contract renewal model, needed as a distinct point of comparison for the one-time-payment-for-permanence design question.

targets.title: Walrus: An Efficient Decentralized Storage Network
targets.authors: George Danezis, Giacomo Giuliari, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Markus Legner, Jean-Pierre Smith, Alberto Sonnino, Karl Wust
targets.venue: arXiv preprint (2025); also published as a systems conference paper
targets.why_needed: 2025 storage-network design using two-dimensional erasure coding (RedStuff) specifically to lower the per-piece repair bandwidth of prior single-dimension erasure-coded designs (Storj, Sia) while tolerating Byzantine (contradictory-message-sending) storage nodes, with a stated storage-overhead figure. Cited by the prior pass at overhead 3.5 against Storj's 1.75; both figures require verification against this paper's own full text before being carried into the evidence file, per the rule against citing prior-pass characterizations as measurements.
